basics.resource_type: PDF design guide (plus web design-guideline pages and blog tutorials from fabrication services, a fastener maker's handbook and a clinching-tool maker's brochures and data sheets)
basics.cost: Free. Protolabs, SendCutSend and TOX pages and PDFs open without login; PEM handbook is a free PDF; Xometry's guide is a free PDF behind a 'Download the Guide' form on its page (the PDF link itself opened directly) [uncertain whether the form asks for an email]
basics.license: All rights reserved for all of them: '© Proto Labs 1999-2026', '© Send Cut Send, Inc.', '© 2025 PennEngineering' (PEM is a registered trademark), TOX data sheets marked 'Subject to technical modifications' with no open licence; Xometry PDF has no licence statement, so treat as all rights reserved [uncertain]. Linking is fine; copying text, tables or drawings is not. Design rules as numbers and facts can be restated in our own words with citation. Wikipedia 'Clinching' is CC BY-SA
basics.language: English (all). TOX publishes in German and other languages and Protolabs has European sites [uncertain: other-language versions not opened]
basics.year: PEM: company founded 1942; handbook edition © 2025. TOX: brochure edition code 80.202604.en (probably April 2026) [uncertain]; design-guideline data sheet 80.18 dated 2022/09; TOX founded 1978 and says it 'invented clinching' (company claim). Protolabs: design-guideline page live in 2026 (© 1999-2026). SendCutSend (established 2018): blog posts dated 5 July 2022, 16 January 2023, 23 July 2025 and 3 September 2025. Xometry: guide page first published 9 October 2020, modified 20 July 2026 (page metadata); PDF v2.2 is older, the 46-page PDF is the current edition. Machine Design article 3 August 2015
basics.access_barrier: none (all open in a normal browser; PDFs download directly). Xometry's main site returned HTTP 429 (rate limit) to scripts, but its design-guide page and PDFs opened. One TOX web page (round joint) redirected to the TOX home page
basics.image_license: All rights reserved (photos, CAD renders, diagrams, section views of clinch joints, fastener drawings). Wikipedia's clinching figures on Commons are openly licensed (e.g. clinching phases image from a CC-licensed journal paper) and an animated GIF 'TOX Pressotechnik Clinching' is on Commons [uncertain: licence of that GIF not checked]
basics.authority_level: manufacturer / service provider: PEM (PennEngineering) and TOX PRESSOTECHNIK are the original makers of self-clinching fasteners and of the TOX clinching process, so they are the primary source for those; Protolabs, Xometry and SendCutSend are commercial fabrication services whose numbers are tuned to their own machines. Wikipedia 'Clinching' cites peer-reviewed papers (e.g. He 2017, 'Clinching for sheet materials')

coverage.covers: Ways to join sheet metal without welding, plus the design rules for the features that make those joints. Tab and slot joints (self-fixturing, locating, poka-yoke keyed tabs), bent/folded tabs that pass through a slot and are folded over, hooks (tab with a notch that drops into the slot edge), key-and-tab (tusk tenon with a wedge key), dog-bone and radiused slots, open, flat and tear-drop hems, curls, offsets (Z-bends), countersinks and dimples, notches and tabs as cut features, corner reliefs, gaps and overlaps at flange corners, self-clinching (press-in) nuts, studs, pins, standoffs, flush fasteners, floating nuts, captive panel screws, locking nuts, non-threaded fasteners, concealed-head, blind, right-angle, cable-tie mounts, sheet-joining fasteners and sealed (ingress protection) studs; POP riveting; clinching (press-joining) with round, flat, SKB (split die), TWINpoint, MICROpoint and Vario-Point joint shapes and eClinching for electrical conduction; and, for contrast, welding (spot, stitch, seam, TIG/MIG), brazing and soldering. Roughly: 4 no-fastener joint types (SendCutSend), about 13 self-clinching fastener types (PEM), 6 clinch point shapes (TOX), and about 10 feature types with rules (Protolabs, Xometry)
coverage.organisation: By feature or process, not by what the user wants. Protolabs and Xometry: by feature (bends, hems, offsets, holes and slots, notches and tabs, countersinks, curls, relief cuts, corner treatments), then finishing, then hardware and assembly (welding, brazing and soldering, mechanical fastening). SendCutSend: blog tutorials, each on one joint idea, with pros/cons summaries; plus guideline pages by service (sheet cutting, bending, hardware, tapping, dimple forming, welding, assembly). PEM: history, how it works, anatomy (nut, stud, standoff), types, installation, problems and solutions, design challenges, Q&A, glossary. TOX: how the joint forms, advantages over spot welding, strength data, point shapes, then design tables. Works reasonably for beginners because each guide is short and illustrated, but nothing starts from 'I need to join these two sheets, what can I use?'
coverage.scope_match: medium: sheet-metal joinery is in scope (lowest priority), and these guides are the authoritative sources for several clever no-weld joint TYPES (tab and slot, folded tab, hook, key-and-wedge, clinching, self-clinching press-in fasteners, hems). Much of the content is general fabrication rules and service-specific tolerances, and the fastener catalogues are standard hardware
coverage.taxonomy_used: No shared taxonomy. Xometry's current guide groups joining under 'Hardware and Assembly' in 3 groups: welding, brazing and soldering, mechanical fastening (inserts: press-fit nuts, press-fit studs, standoffs, captive screws, cable-tie mounts). PEM: 3 basic styles of self-clinching (nut with serrated clinching ring, stud with ribs, standoff/hex-head) and 13 functional types (nuts; studs and pins; spacers and standoffs; flush fasteners; floating nuts; threaded access hardware; locking fasteners; non-threaded fasteners; concealed-head; blind; right angle; cable tie-mount; sheet joining fastener; ingress protection). TOX: by point shape (Round Joint, Flat Point, SKB split die, TWINpoint, MICROpoint, Vario-Point). Wikipedia 'Clinching': round tools (fixed grooved die, split die with 2-4 movable sectors, flat die) versus rectangular tools (sheared). SendCutSend: 4 fastener-free joints (tab and slot, bent tabs, hooks, key and tab)
coverage.example_types: tab and slot joint (self-fixturing locator); keyed or varied-width tabs (poka-yoke, mistake-proofing); plug-welded tab (for contrast); bent tab / folded tab through a slot (tab bent over after insertion); twisted tab [uncertain: named only in a search summary, not on an opened page]; hook and slot (notched tab that drops into the slot edge); key-and-tab / tusk tenon with a wedge key; dog-bone slot (stress-relief holes at slot corners); open hem, flat (closed) hem and tear-drop hem; curl (rolled edge); offset / joggle (Z-bend); clinch joint (press-joining, 'riveting without rivets'); round clinch joint and flat clinch point; split-die (SKB) clinch; twin-point clinch (anti-rotation); miniature clinch point (2 mm); Vario-Point clinch through a pre-punched sheet for hard or non-ductile materials; eClinching (electrically conductive clinch); self-clinching nut (press-in nut, PEM nut); self-clinching stud and pin; self-clinching standoff; floating self-clinching nut (allows hole misalignment); captive panel screw (threaded access hardware); self-clinching locking nut; right-angle self-clinching fastener (replaces bent tabs and brackets); sheet-joining self-clinching fastener; dimple-formed countersink; POP (blind) rivet
coverage.making_methods: Sheet metal: laser, waterjet and plasma cutting, CNC press-brake bending, punching, hardware insertion presses, clinching presses and tongs; also laser/CNC-router cut sheet materials in general (SendCutSend's tab and slot advice covers routed composites and notes dog-bones for router corners). Hobby makers using online cut-and-bend services, and industrial production (automotive, appliance, HVAC, enclosures)
coverage.item_count: PEM handbook 20 pages with 13 fastener types; TOX brochure 11 pages with 6 point shapes and a data sheet of 11 pages with design tables for point diameters 2-12 mm; Xometry current guide 46 pages (older v2.2 12 pages); Protolabs guidelines page with 6 feature tabs (bend radius, hems, offsets, holes and slots, notches and tabs, countersinks); SendCutSend 4 joint types in its no-fastener article and over 100 PEM hardware parts in its hardware service
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: hand-release only / removable: yes (SendCutSend: tab and slot 'great if your design needs to be frequently disassembled', key-and-tab 'the key can be removed', hooks can be undone 'with enough force'; PEM captive panel screws stay with the door; Xometry notes mechanical fastening makes removable joints). self-locking: yes (hooks, wedge keys that clamp more the further they are tapped in, PEM locking nuts with prevailing torque). one-way / permanent: yes (bent tabs, clinching and self-clinching fasteners are permanent). indexing/detent: no. over-centre: no. compliant: partly (SendCutSend: a flexible key 'can even be designed to snap into place, much like a buckle') . print-in-place: no. gear trains: no. powered connectors: no (only powered installation presses). torque-limiting: no. adhesive types: little (TOX: clinching can be combined with adhesives or intermediate layers; SendCutSend: 'adding a drop or two of glue' stiffens a tab and slot joint)
coverage.entry_structure: Feature name, one-paragraph explanation, labelled diagram, rule-of-thumb dimensions in multiples of material thickness (t) or absolute sizes, and tolerance tables (Protolabs, Xometry). SendCutSend adds flat-pattern and assembled images, tips and a pros/cons summary per joint. PEM: cut-away anatomy drawings, material hardness tables, step-by-step installation pictures, do's and don'ts, troubleshooting, glossary. TOX: step sequence of joint formation (penetration, compression, emergence of contour, lateral spreading), section drawing with 'control dimension X', strength graphs and design tables
coverage.audience_level: professional (product and mechanical designers, fabricators) and hobbyist (SendCutSend explicitly targets makers and small shops). TOX data sheets are for production engineers

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: medium: SendCutSend is high (plain language, photos, pros/cons, 'simply bend the tab by hand or with pliers'); Protolabs and Xometry are medium (clear rules but terse, assume you know 'flange', 'relief', 'K-factor'); PEM is medium (very clear anatomy and Q&A plus a glossary, but industrial); TOX is low (production data sheets, material grade codes like DC01, DX51D)
usefulness.has_images: yes: good diagrams throughout (Protolabs feature images, Xometry labelled dimension drawings, SendCutSend flat-pattern and assembly figures and photos, PEM cut-away drawings, TOX section views and point-shape photos)
usefulness.has_animations: yes, some video: SendCutSend links a video guide to tab and slot design and has a YouTube channel ('Cutting Corners' episodes); TOX has videos on its site and an animated clinching GIF is on Wikimedia Commons [uncertain: TOX videos not opened]. No interactive models
usefulness.gaps: No selector that starts from the need ('permanent or removable?', 'do I have a press?', 'how thick?'); lanced (cut-and-formed) tabs, twist tabs, louver/lance locks and lock seams (Pittsburgh lock, standing seam) are barely covered by these five sources; hems are treated as safe edges, not as joints; clinching and self-clinching need a press, which most hobbyists lack, and hand alternatives (hand clinching pliers, hammer-in or rivet nuts) are not compared; numbers are specific to each service's machines and differ (e.g. open-hem return length 6t at Protolabs vs 4t at Xometry); little strength data for the no-fastener joints (tab, hook, key)
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: Yes: SendCutSend blog posts and Protolabs design-tip pages have stable readable URLs (e.g. https://sendcutsend.com/blog/how-to-join-laser-cut-parts-without-fasteners/ for tab/hook/key joints). PEM handbook and TOX data sheets are stable-looking PDF URLs on the makers' asset servers, but asset URLs with random ids may change [uncertain]. Protolabs guideline sections are tabs on one page, so no per-feature anchor URL was seen
usefulness.reusable_data: Not reusable as data (all rights reserved, no API). The design rules (e.g. minimum flange 4t, tab width at least 2t or 3.2 mm, clinch edge distance) are facts that can be restated with citation. SendCutSend's hardware catalogue and PEM's online catalogue are browsable per part but scrape-only
usefulness.maintained: Yes: Protolabs (© 2026), Xometry guide modified July 2026, SendCutSend posts to 2025 and site current, PEM handbook © 2025, TOX brochure edition 2026 [uncertain]. The Machine Design 2015 gallery is still online. Older Xometry v2.2 PDF is superseded but still online
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: 1) SendCutSend's per-joint pros/cons box ('Pros: simplest and easiest to assemble; Con: not effective for thin and flexible materials') is ideal for encyclopedia entries. 2) Express rules as multiples of material thickness (t), e.g. 'tab at least 2t', 'hole at least 2t from an edge', which beginners can apply to any sheet. 3) PEM's three-drawing anatomy (nut, stud, standoff) and its do's-and-don'ts list. 4) TOX's step strip showing how a joint forms (penetration, compression, spreading) is a good template for animating any press-formed joint. 5) Poka-yoke idea: vary tab widths so a part only fits one way. 6) A 'choose by what you have' filter: hand-bendable (bent tabs, hooks, keys) vs press needed (clinching, self-clinching) vs welder needed. 7) PEM's glossary as a model for our own plain-English glossary
usefulness.design_rules_given: Yes, many numbers. Protolabs: minimum flange length 4t; open hem inside diameter at least t with return length 6t; tabs at least 2t or 0.126 in (3.2 mm) wide, no longer than 5x width; notches at least t or 0.04 in (1 mm), no longer than 5x width; features within about 4t of a bend may deform; PEM hardware edge distance per PEM catalogue 'min. distance hole C/L to edge'; bend angle tolerance ±1 degree. Xometry v2.2: open and tear-drop hem return at least 4t, tear-drop opening at least t/4, curls outside radius at least 2t, holes at least 2t from an edge and 2.5t plus bend radius from a bend, slots 4t plus bend radius from a bend, corner fillet t/2; brazing gap 0.05-0.2 mm. SendCutSend: slip-fit slot = tab + 0.010 in in width and thickness; tolerance 0.003 in per side for 0.060 in sheet, 0.005 in for 0.125 in, 0.010-0.020 in for 0.250 in plate; powder coat adds 0.002-0.005 in per surface; tab length 0.5-0.75 of mating part depth; bent tabs for sheet under 0.080 in; router dog-bones 0.063 in radius. PEM: fasteners work in sheet as thin as 0.008 in (0.2 mm), usually 0.030-0.040 in minimum; hole tolerance +0.003/-0 in (+0.08 mm); maximum sheet hardness table (e.g. aluminium fasteners under HRB 50, hardened stainless under HRB 88); multi-fastener spacing = C/L-to-edge + half the second hole diameter. TOX: sheets 0.1-12 mm, point diameters 2-26 mm; clinch strength up to about 70% of a spot weld and about 40% cheaper; design table for point diameters 2-12 mm with edge distance (2-10 mm), point-to-point distance (4-20 mm) and total sheet thickness ranges (0.3-11 mm); control dimension X tolerance ±15%. Machine Design: bend tabs perpendicular to rolling direction or at least 45 degrees to it (its thickness range '0.12 to 0.8 in' looks like a typo for 0.012-0.08 in) [uncertain]
usefulness.generator_or_parametric: Partly: SendCutSend's Parts Builder (customisable part templates) and its app that auto-sizes holes when hardware is chosen; SolidWorks Toolbox includes PEM fasteners (as described by SendCutSend); PEM and SendCutSend offer downloadable fastener CAD models. No generators for joint geometry (e.g. tab-and-slot generators) in these sources
usefulness.file_formats: PDF (Xometry, PEM, TOX, Protolabs white paper/toolkit), HTML pages, video (YouTube), CAD models of fasteners (PEM catalogue downloads) [uncertain: formats not checked]; the services accept DXF, DWG, AI, EPS and STEP uploads
usefulness.terminology_value: High for sheet-metal terms and aliases: clinching = clinch joining = press-joining = 'toxing' = 'riveting without rivets'; self-clinching fastener = press-fit / press-in insert = PEM nut; open / closed (flat) / tear-drop hem; curl; offset; relief; dog-bone; tusk tenon; poka-yoke; cold flow, undercut, knurled clinching ring, floating, captive (PEM glossary). English only
usefulness.decision_support: Limited: comparison tables rather than a selector. Xometry has tables of weld types (appearance, use case, cost impact) and of insert types (function, key advantage, application); TOX compares clinching with spot welding and riveting (cost, energy, fatigue strength); SendCutSend gives pros/cons per joint; Protolabs lists possible solutions with rationale for features near bends; PEM gives do's/don'ts and a troubleshooting section. No flow chart
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: Overlaps with the existing '3D printing service design guides (Hubs, Protolabs, Xometry, Formlabs, Prusa)' item (same companies, different process), with 'DIN 8593 joining process classification' (clinching is 'joining by forming' there), 'Joining and selection tools (TWI, Swift and Booker, Granta EduPack)', 'Digital joinery catalogues' and 'Boxes.py' (laser-cut finger and tab joints) and the McMaster-Carr/MISUMI supplier catalogue item (self-clinching hardware). PEM (PennEngineering) is the original source for self-clinching fasteners (founded 1942 by K.A. Swanstrom); Protolabs, Xometry and SendCutSend all defer to PEM's catalogue for hole sizes and edge distances. TOX claims to have invented clinching; Wikipedia 'Clinching' gives the neutral overview and academic references
